questions.q: What does a fuzz test check that a fixed-input unit test cannot?
options: Edge cases across hundreds of randomized inputs, which a handful of hand-picked numbers would never stumble into
Whether the Solidity compiler itself has bugs
Nothing — fuzz tests and unit tests check exactly the same thing
Whether the frontend's CSS renders correctly
questions.explain: A fuzz test runs the same function many times with randomized inputs (clamped with bound()), which surfaces edge cases that fixed, hand-picked unit test values would never happen to hit.

questions.q: What does invariant_BalanceMatchesReserves actually verify in this lesson's example?
options: That the pool's real token balance never falls below what its own reserve bookkeeping claims, after any sequence of calls
That the frontend displays the correct font size
That gas prices stay below a fixed threshold
That the contract was deployed exactly once
questions.explain: Using targetContract to generate randomized call sequences, this invariant checks tokenA/tokenB balanceOf the pool against reserveA/reserveB after any sequence of operations — exactly the class of accounting bug that causes an insolvent pool.

questions.q: Which security-review item does this lesson say should be stated explicitly as an intentional design choice, not an oversight?
options: The absence of access control, since this pool is intentionally permissionless
The presence of two ERC-20 tokens
The use of Solidity 0.8
The existence of a addLiquidity function
questions.explain: The lesson calls out that 'no access control' should be documented as a deliberate decision for a permissionless pool, not left looking like something the author forgot to add.

questions.q: What known gap does this lesson's checklist flag regarding swaps, carried over from Lesson 4?
options: The absence of a minAmountOut slippage parameter, leaving swaps open to being sandwiched or front-run
The absence of any token reserves at all
The contract's inability to compile
The lack of a contract name
questions.explain: The lesson restates Lesson 4's flagged gap: without a minAmountOut parameter, a swap transaction can be sandwiched or front-run for a worse price than the quoted preview.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend emitting Swap and LiquidityAdded events from the pool's state-changing functions?
options: Without events, reconstructing swap/liquidity history means replaying every block by hand, the same indexing problem covered in the backend material
Events are required by the Solidity compiler for the contract to deploy
Events replace the need for any tests
Events automatically prevent reentrancy
questions.explain: Events give an indexer (or a subgraph) an efficient way to reconstruct activity like swap and liquidity history, instead of needing to replay the entire chain's blocks manually.
